Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
The phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience is fundamentally distinct from the mere expression of personal liking, as it inherently involves a claim to intersubjective validity. When an observer encounters a work of profound beauty, the resulting judgment is not experienced as a private, idiosyncratic reaction akin to a preference for a particular flavor of food. Rather, to judge a work as beautiful is to make a claim that extends beyond the self, implicitly calling upon others to share in the same appreciation. This normative dimension is built into the very grammar of aesthetic pronouncements; we do not merely report our internal psychological states by saying that a work pleases us, but instead attribute a value to the work itself, expecting that any similarly situated observer ought to recognize this quality. A purely subjectivist framework is entirely unable to explain this felt demand for agreement, as it reduces all aesthetic judgments to autobiographical reports of pleasure, thereby erasing the distinctively normative weight that characterizes our actual encounters with art.

This claim to validity is not a mere psychological illusion but is actively sustained by the collective practice of aesthetic criticism, which presupposes that evaluations are answerable to considerations beyond individual response. The entire institution of criticism—with its reliance on reasons, formal standards, and the cultivation of taste through education—operates on the assumption that some aesthetic assessments are objectively better-informed, more perceptive, and more coherent than others. When a critic defends an evaluation, they do not simply describe their feelings; they direct our attention to specific, observable features of the artwork, such as its structural harmony, thematic depth, or innovative technique, demonstrating how these elements justify a particular interpretation and valuation. If aesthetic value were nothing more than a projection of subjective preference, the concepts of aesthetic education and the refinement of taste would be meaningless, as there would be no standard against which to measure progress or to distinguish a mature, deeply considered judgment from a superficial one.

Furthermore, any attempt to escape these objective demands through aesthetic relativism inevitably generates a self-defeating logical regress that undermines the position from within. The relativist argues that because all aesthetic judgments are ultimately grounded in subjective preference, no single standard of taste can claim authority over another, meaning that a pluralistic tolerance of all preferences is the only coherent stance. However, this insistence on pluralism and the rejection of dogmatism is itself a value judgment, representing a specific preference for open-mindedness over hierarchical exclusion. If the relativist’s primary assertion is true—that all preferences are merely subjective psychological states with no objective validity—then their own preference for pluralism is likewise nothing more than an arbitrary, subjective whim. To claim that pluralism is the correct or superior approach is to appeal to an objective standard of validity that the relativist’s own theory denies, while to admit that pluralism is merely one arbitrary preference among others is to strip the relativist position of any normative force, reducing it to a hollow assertion that cannot coherently defend itself against dogmatism.

--- RESPONSE B ---
When one experiences a work of art as genuinely beautiful, the judgment carries with it an implicit demand that others ought to share in that appreciation, rather than treating the response as a mere private sensation. This phenomenological feature of aesthetic experience points to a normative claim of intersubjective validity, suggesting that the beauty is there to be recognized by any suitably attuned perceiver. A framework that reduces aesthetic value entirely to subjective preference struggles to account for this dimension, as it would render such calls for agreement inexplicable or merely rhetorical. 

The ongoing practices of aesthetic criticism rely on the possibility of offering reasons and appealing to standards that transcend individual tastes, allowing for education in appreciation and the distinction between more and less informed responses. Critics engage in detailed analysis and comparison precisely because they assume that assessments can be improved through attention to relevant features of the work, rather than being insulated within personal psychology. This institutional reality indicates that aesthetic judgments are responsive to considerations that can be shared and debated, undermining any strict reduction to isolated subjective states.

The position of aesthetic relativism encounters an internal difficulty, for if all preferences are deemed equally valid without further grounding, then the relativist's own advocacy for tolerance or pluralism over rigid dogmatism amounts to nothing more than another preference without special authority. This creates a regress in which the normative force required to sustain the relativist stance against alternative views cannot be consistently maintained, revealing the position's inability to provide a coherent alternative to objectivist understandings of aesthetic value.

--- RESPONSE C ---
The phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience reveals an inherent claim to intersubjective validity, a feature that undermines purely subjectivist accounts of aesthetic value. When we judge a work of art beautiful, we do not merely report a private sensation; we implicitly demand that others ought to recognize its beauty as well. This normative dimension—the expectation of shared agreement—cannot be explained if aesthetic judgment is reduced to arbitrary personal preference. The very act of making an aesthetic claim carries an appeal to a standard beyond the self, suggesting that beauty is not merely "in the eye of the beholder" but involves a recognition of qualities that transcend individual psychology. If aesthetic value were wholly subjective, the disappointment we feel when others fail to appreciate what we find beautiful would be unintelligible, yet such disappointment is a common and meaningful feature of aesthetic engagement. The intersubjective pull of aesthetic judgment points to a shared realm of value that cannot be collapsed into isolated subjective responses.

The practice of aesthetic criticism further demonstrates that assessments of art are not reducible to individual taste alone. Criticism operates within a framework of reasons, standards, and cultivated discernment, presupposing that some interpretations and evaluations are more defensible than others. Critics do not merely catalogue personal reactions; they appeal to principles of composition, historical context, technical skill, and imaginative depth, arguing that certain works reward attention more richly than others. This discursive practice would be incoherent if all aesthetic responses were equally valid, since the very act of offering justification implies that some judgments are better grounded. Moreover, the tradition of aesthetic education—the belief that exposure to great art refines perception—relies on the assumption that discernment can be developed and that some ways of engaging with art are more informed than others. If aesthetic value were purely subjective, the notion of "better-informed" responses would be meaningless, yet the entire enterprise of criticism and education depends on this possibility.

Aesthetic relativism, taken to its logical conclusion, undermines itself through a regress that exposes its normative emptiness. If all aesthetic preferences are equally valid, then the relativist's own preference for pluralism over dogmatism is itself just another arbitrary stance, lacking any special authority. The relativist cannot consistently claim that tolerance is superior to intolerance without appealing to a standard that transcends individual preference, yet such an appeal contradicts the core premise of relativism. This internal contradiction reveals that the relativist position cannot sustain its own normative aspirations—it cannot defend the value of openness without implicitly appealing to a criterion that relativism explicitly denies. The regress demonstrates that any attempt to assert the universal validity of relativism collapses into self-refutation, leaving no coherent way to privilege one aesthetic stance over another. The very act of advocating for relativism presupposes a normative framework that relativism itself cannot accommodate, exposing its inadequacy as a comprehensive account of aesthetic value.

--- RESPONSE D ---
Aesthetic value cannot be coherently reduced to purely subjective preference because the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience already exceeds the structure of mere liking. When someone judges a work beautiful, moving, graceful, profound, or artistically successful, the judgment is not ordinarily experienced as a private report equivalent to “this happens to please me.” It carries an implicit appeal to others, as though the object itself merits appreciation. To call a painting beautiful is not simply to describe one’s psychological state before it; it is to present the work as worthy of admiration. The judgment therefore has a normative and intersubjective character: it asks, or at least invites, others to see what one sees. This does not mean that everyone must in fact agree, but it does mean that aesthetic judgment presents itself as more than autobiographical preference. A purely subjectivist framework can register the occurrence of pleasure, attraction, excitement, or aversion, but it cannot explain why aesthetic language so naturally takes the form of appraisal rather than confession. The difference between “I like this” and “this is beautiful” is not merely grammatical; it marks the difference between reporting an individual response and making a claim that aspires to shared recognition.

The same point is confirmed by the practice of aesthetic criticism. Criticism would be unintelligible if aesthetic assessments were nothing more than isolated psychological events. Critics do not merely announce their reactions; they give reasons, draw comparisons, invoke genre, form, proportion, originality, expressive power, historical context, technical achievement, coherence, subtlety, and depth. They attempt to show why a work succeeds or fails, and their arguments can be more or less perceptive, informed, disciplined, or shallow. The very existence of aesthetic education presupposes that taste can be cultivated and that perception can be refined. One can learn to hear structural complexity in music, to notice compositional balance in painting, to recognize dramatic economy in theater, or to appreciate allusion and rhythm in poetry. Such learning does not simply produce new private preferences; it enables better attention to features of the work. If all responses were equally authoritative merely because they occurred, there would be no meaningful distinction between a hasty reaction and a trained judgment, between inattentiveness and insight, between missing what is present in a work and responding to it with understanding. The institutions and practices of criticism therefore presuppose that aesthetic value is answerable to considerations beyond the brute fact of individual response.

Aesthetic relativism also undermines itself from within. If every aesthetic preference is equally valid simply because it is someone’s preference, then no preference can claim superiority over any other, including the preference for tolerance, pluralism, or openness. The relativist who treats all tastes as equally legitimate typically presents this stance as preferable to dogmatism, narrowness, or authoritarian judgment. But if relativism is true in the strong sense that aesthetic positions have no validity beyond the preferences of individuals or communities, then the valuation of pluralism is itself merely one preference among others. It has no greater normative standing than the dogmatism it rejects. The relativist cannot coherently say that we ought to be pluralistic, receptive, or nonjudgmental, because “ought” introduces precisely the kind of normativity that radical subjectivism dissolves. Thus the view consumes its own authority: it seeks to establish a normative conclusion while denying the grounds on which any such conclusion could be binding. Aesthetic value must therefore involve more than subjective preference, because even the attempt to deny this relies on standards of better and worse, more and less adequate, more and less defensible ways of responding.

--- RESPONSE E ---
Aesthetic judgment, examined closely, resists any clean reduction to the private flutterings of individual taste. When we call a painting beautiful, a symphony profound, or a novel masterful, we are not merely reporting an inner weather, as one might report feeling warm or craving salt. The grammar and phenomenology of such judgments diverge sharply from the grammar of avowed preference. To find Vermeer's Woman Holding a Balance beautiful is to experience something in the work itself as calling for recognition; the judgment arrives with a felt pressure outward, a tacit summons to others. Kant captured this structure in his observation that aesthetic judgments, though grounded in feeling, speak with a universal voice: we do not say merely that the work pleases us but that it is beautiful, and in doing so we implicitly expect, and even demand, agreement. This is why aesthetic disagreement feels substantively different from disagreement about ice cream flavors. Someone who dislikes pistachio owes no account of themselves; someone who dismisses Bach as noise invites, and seems to deserve, challenge. The subjectivist framework, which treats aesthetic utterances as disguised reports of private response, cannot accommodate this normative texture without explaining it away, and explaining it away requires treating the phenomenology of countless competent judges as systematically illusory, a cost that should give pause to anyone attentive to what aesthetic experience is actually like.

This normative structure is not merely a feature of first-person experience; it is institutionalized in the practice of criticism, which would be unintelligible if aesthetic assessments were merely autobiographical. Critics offer reasons: they point to the handling of color, the architecture of a sonata-allegro, the moral intelligence of a characterization, the way a line of verse enacts what it describes. These reasons are offered as reasons, as considerations that ought to move a suitably attentive reader or viewer, not as idiosyncratic triggers for the critic's private pleasure. Correspondingly, aesthetic education exists and makes sense: we train the ear to hear counterpoint, the eye to register compositional balance, the mind to track narrative irony, and we take this training to improve, not merely to alter, aesthetic response. The practice draws distinctions between the connoisseur and the novice, between the judgment formed in ignorance and the judgment formed through sustained engagement with tradition, technique, and context. A response grounded in attentive familiarity with Shakespeare's uses of soliloquy is better-informed than one grounded in a half-remembered high school encounter, and this is not a snobbish prejudice but a presupposition without which the entire enterprise of criticism, teaching, curation, and canon-formation collapses into incoherence. If all responses were equally valid qua responses, there would be nothing for the critic to do but publish diaries, and no reason to prefer one diary to another.

The thoroughgoing aesthetic relativist, who affirms that every preference stands on equal footing, confronts a further difficulty that arises from within the position itself. The relativist typically commends their view on broadly normative grounds: pluralism is more tolerant, more humble, more respectful of difference, less tyrannical than any aesthetic dogmatism that would elevate some responses above others. But if aesthetic judgments reduce to preference, so too, by any consistent extension, does the meta-level preference for pluralism over dogmatism. The relativist's commendation of their own stance can then possess no more rational authority than the dogmatist's commendation of theirs; it is simply what the relativist happens to favor. The regress is immediate: whatever normative weight is claimed for relativism must either be denied, in which case the position becomes a mere confession of taste that others are free to ignore, or affirmed, in which case the relativist has conceded that at least some evaluative judgments carry force beyond individual response and has thereby abandoned the very thesis under defense. The position, pressed, consumes its own ground, and this self-undermining structure suggests that the normativity the relativist cannot escape at the meta-level is the same normativity that was present, all along, in the first-order aesthetic judgments the theory sought to dissolve.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
